analysis.one_liner: Repeals the law requiring mortgage lenders to disclose who they lend to and where.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act was introduced in September 2015, referred to the House Financial Services Committee, and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act off the books. That 1975 law requires banks and mortgage lenders to report publicly who they make home loans to, where, at what cost, and who they turn down. Regulators, researchers, and community groups use that data to spot lending discrimination and neighborhoods being cut off from credit. Repealing it would remove that public record, leaving lenders with far less outside scrutiny of their lending patterns.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks and mortgage lenders would benefit. They would no longer have to compile and file detailed public reports on every home loan application, and their lending decisions in particular neighborhoods would no longer be visible to regulators and the public. Compliance costs for lenders, especially smaller ones, would disappear.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act of 1975 in its entirety, ending the requirement that covered lenders disclose their mortgage lending data to the public.

Makes conforming changes to related laws, including the Federal Home Loan Bank Act, the Housing and Community Development Act of 1992, and the Dodd-Frank Act, to strip out references to and data-collection requirements tied to the disclosure law.

analysis.who_pays: Homebuyers and communities. Without lender-by-lender, neighborhood-by-neighborhood loan data, it becomes much harder to detect discrimination in lending, 'redlining' of minority neighborhoods, and lenders steering borrowers into costlier loans. Fair-lending enforcers and community advocates lose their main data source; borrowers in underserved areas lose the visibility that helps bring credit back.

drawbacks.text: HMDA reporting imposes real paperwork and compliance costs on lenders, which smaller banks and credit unions have long argued is burdensome and, for some data fields, redundant with other regulators' requirements.

Supporters of repeal argued that public disclosure of loan data serves little purpose for ordinary borrowers; the counterargument is that the data's value is not to individual borrowers but to regulators and community groups policing discrimination, and the bill offered no replacement for that function.
Repealing the law outright, rather than streamlining reporting for smaller lenders, would eliminate the data entirely — including the census-tract-level data that fair-lending enforcement relies on.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is lower compliance costs for lenders; the main cost is the loss of the primary public dataset used to detect mortgage discrimination and disinvestment in particular neighborhoods. Weighed honestly, the benefit flows narrowly to the regulated industry while the cost falls broadly on borrowers and communities, with no replacement mechanism in the bill.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Dave Brat introduced the HMDA Repeal Act of 2015 on September 18, 2015, with the bill referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services.
The bill repeal the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act of 1975 in full, ending public mortgage-lending disclosure requirements.
The committee never reported the bill and no vote was ever scheduled on it; the action history shows no activity after the initial referral.
The disclosure law the bill targeted remained in effect, so lenders kept their reporting obligations and the public mortgage-lending dataset remained available through the end of the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, nothing changed: mortgage lenders kept their disclosure obligations, and borrowers and communities kept the transparency the law provides. Lenders avoided new scrutiny, but they also gained nothing; the outcome simply preserved the status quo in favor of the public.

for.name: Rep. Dave Brat
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act and referred it to committee.

for.name: Rep. Steve Chabot
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the repeal bill as an original cosponsor.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it was never scheduled for a markup or a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only Republican sponsorship and two Republican cosponsors, but it never advanced far enough for a party-line split to show up in any vote.

industries.note: Repeal would end lenders' public reporting of who gets home loans, where, and at what cost, eliminating their main public transparency obligation. Lenders' interest in less visibility runs against borrowers' interest in having lending discrimination and redlining exposed.

These groups rely on HMDA data to identify neighborhoods denied credit and lenders with discriminatory patterns; repeal would take away their core dataset and weaken their ability to hold lenders accountable.
